etymology: An ordinary English compound (jaw + line) for the outline of the lower face, made a fixation by the looksmaxxing culture of the late 2010s and 2020s, which treats a sharp, square jaw as the master key to male attractiveness. Gen Alpha boys post "jawline checks," practice mewing (a tongue-posture technique claimed to reshape the jaw), chew hard silicone jaw-trainers, and turn their heads in photos to show the angle; "his jawline is crazy" is high praise and "no jawline" a taunt.
biblical_def: In Gen Alpha talk, a good jawline is one of the most important things a boy can have — sharp, square, "mogging" the other guys. Boys as young as ten post jawline pictures, practice mewing, and worry that their faces are not good enough. The Christian observation: Scripture says plainly that God is not impressed by the things we measure in mirrors. "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy" (Psa 147:10-11). The Messiah Himself, in Isaiah’s portrait, had "no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him" (Isa 53:2) — the most important face in history was not a jawline face. Caring for the body is good — "bodily exercise profiteth little" (1Ti 4:8), and little is not nothing — but a boy who studies his jaw more than his heart is training for the wrong contest. A father can tell a five-year-old son: "God made your face just right. What He cares about most is your heart — are you kind, are you brave, do you love Him?" And to the twelve-year-old: "The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him" — that is the measurement that counts.
webster_summary: Ordinary word for the lower face’s outline, made a looksmaxxing obsession (2010s–2020s) for boys — a measure of worth God says He takes no pleasure in, beside the fear of Him that He does.
webster_full: JAWLINE, n. (English; Gen Alpha / looksmaxxing usage, 2010s–present) The outline of the lower jaw, prized when sharp and square. "Bro’s jawline is insane."
Related: mewing, mogging, looksmaxxing, jawline check, jaw trainer.
Decode for parents: boys are being taught to grade their faces; ask what your son thinks of his.
Webster 1828, the root — JAW, n. The bones of the mouth in which the teeth are fixed.
scriptures: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.
The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy.
Isa 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: The jawline fixation teaches boys that their worth is in the angle of their bones; Scripture says the LORD takes no pleasure in the legs of a man but in them that fear Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Looksmaxxing arrived in boys’ lives through edits, gym content, and online forums whose roots lie in incel culture, where the face is fate. The jawline is its central icon. Boys who absorb it begin to see themselves and others as faces to be ranked, and some fall into anxiety, compulsive mirror-checking, and despair over features they cannot change.

Answer with both care and truth. It is good for a boy to be strong, clean, and well-kept; it is ruinous for him to locate his worth in his jaw. Tell him often what you admire in his character, model contentment with your own aging face, and give him Psalm 147. The face God loves best is the one turned toward Him.

2020s: jawline checks, jaw trainers, head-turned photo poses
Related: mogging, mewing, canthal tilt, hunter eyes
usage: "Do you think my jawline’s good?" "I think your heart’s good. That’s what I see."
He taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man — nor in his jawline (Psa 147:10).
He had no form nor comeliness — the face that saved the world (Isa 53:2).

etymology: A medical and cosmetic term: the angle of the line from the inner corner of the eye (the medial canthus, from Greek kanthos) to the outer corner. A "positive" tilt, with the outer corner higher, is prized in looksmaxxing forums as a sign of attractiveness; a "negative" tilt is mocked. Around 2023 TikTok filters and videos taught children to measure their own canthal tilt, and the word passed from surgeons’ charts into Gen Alpha vocabulary, along with talk of "fixing" it surgically.
biblical_def: A canthal tilt is the angle of your eyes — whether the outside corners point up or down. Looksmaxxing videos teach kids to measure it and say that "positive" tilt is attractive and "negative" tilt is ugly. Some children now hold rulers to their faces in the mirror. The Christian observation: this is a child measuring the work of God’s hands and finding fault with it. Scripture has a word for the clay that criticizes the potter: "Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?" (Isa 45:9). David said the opposite about his own body: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works" (Psa 139:14), and "in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned" (Psa 139:16). Eyes in Scripture are for seeing, not for being graded: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). A father can tell a five-year-old: "God made your eyes exactly the way He wanted, and they’re beautiful because He made them. Your eyes are for seeing all the wonderful things He made!" And to a teen who has been measuring: "Throw away the ruler. Your Maker already said what He thinks."
webster_summary: Surgeons’ term for the eye-corner angle, taught to children by looksmaxxing filters (c. 2023) — the clay measuring the potter’s work and finding fault, against "fearfully and wonderfully made."
webster_full: CANTHAL TILT, n. (medical / cosmetic term; looksmaxxing and Gen Alpha usage, c. 2023–present) The angle between the inner and outer corners of the eye; "positive" (outer corner higher) is prized. "I have negative canthal tilt."
From Greek kanthos, corner of the eye.
Related: hunter eyes, prey eyes, looksmaxxing, canthoplasty (eye-corner surgery).
Decode for parents: if your child knows this term, she has been taught to grade her face; respond with care.
scriptures: Isa 45:9
Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
corruption_summary: Canthal-tilt talk teaches children to measure their faces against a forum’s chart and despise what they cannot change; Scripture calls that striving with one’s Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Of all the looksmaxxing vocabulary, this is perhaps the most purely destructive for a child, because the feature it grades cannot be changed by diet, exercise, or effort — only by surgery. Its lesson is fatalism: you were born ugly or not, and the chart says which. That is the incel forums’ "blackpill" philosophy in a child’s mouth.

Reject the measurement and replace it with praise. Read Psalm 139 aloud to a child who has learned this word. Tell her that her eyes were written in God’s book before she was born. And if a child’s self-hatred over a feature seems deep, take it as seriously as any other grief — pray with her, talk often, and get help.

etymology: Looksmaxxing jargon from 2010s online forums, much of it incel-adjacent: hunter eyes are deep-set, hooded, narrow eyes with a positive canthal tilt and little visible upper eyelid, said to look intense, dominant, and predatory; their opposite, prey eyes, are rounder, more open, and said to look weak. The terms spread through TikTok and "sigma" edits around 2023, with certain actors held up as models, and Gen Alpha boys now describe each other’s eyes as hunter or prey.
biblical_def: Hunter eyes are supposed to be the "best" eyes for a guy — deep, narrow, and intense, like a predator’s — while open, friendly eyes get called "prey eyes." Gen Alpha boys now look at each other’s faces and sort them that way. The Christian observation: the terms divide the world into hunters and prey, and that picture is very old, and very wicked. The Psalmist describes the predator’s eyes: "he sitteth in the lurking places of the villages... his eyes are privily set against the poor" (Psa 10:8). Scripture does not want our eyes to look like a predator’s; it wants them clean. Job said, "I made a covenant with mine eyes" (Job 31:1), and Jesus said, "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). And it tells every child his eyes, whatever their shape, were God’s design: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14). A father can tell a five-year-old: "God doesn’t make ‘hunter’ and ‘prey’ people. He made all of us, and He wants our eyes to be kind and full of light — the kind that look out for others." And to the twelve-year-old: "The world wants you to look dangerous. God wants you to be safe for the weak to stand near."
webster_summary: Incel-adjacent looksmaxxing jargon (2010s; TikTok c. 2023) sorting eyes into predator and prey — a hunter-and-victim picture of the world that Scripture assigns to the wicked man lying in wait.
webster_full: HUNTER EYES, n. (looksmaxxing jargon, 2010s; Gen Alpha usage, c. 2023–present) Deep-set, hooded, narrow eyes with positive canthal tilt, prized as intense and dominant. Opposite: prey eyes. "He’s got hunter eyes."
Related: canthal tilt, mogging, looksmaxxing, sigma face.
Decode for parents: the vocabulary comes from forums that teach boys their faces are their fate.
Webster 1828, the root — HUNTER, n. A dog that scents game, or is employed in the chase.
scriptures: Psa 10:8
He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor.
Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: "Hunter eyes" grades faces by how predatory they look and sorts boys into hunters and prey; Scripture gives the predator’s eyes to the wicked and asks for eyes that are single and full of light.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary is not neutral beauty talk; it is a worldview. Its picture of manhood is predation — the hunter who dominates — and its picture of the gentle is "prey." Boys who absorb it learn to admire a dangerous look and to despise an open, friendly face. That is a small step toward admiring dangerous men.

Reject the frame and offer Christ’s. The Good Shepherd’s eyes are not a hunter’s; they are a guardian’s. Teach your son that real strength protects the weak, that his eyes are for seeing others’ needs, and that his face was God’s design. A man who is safe for children to stand near is a better man than any "hunter."

His eyes are privily set against the poor — that’s the real hunter (Psa 10:8).

etymology: A 2023–24 TikTok coinage, from the image of a person whose back has grown wide from overeating: a big back is someone who eats a lot, and big back behavior is ordering extra, eating late at night, or getting excited about food. Gen Alpha uses it jokingly of themselves ("I’m being big back") and mockingly of others, where it slides into fat-shaming.
biblical_def: In Gen Alpha slang, a big back is somebody who eats a lot — "big back behavior" is getting a third slice of pizza or raiding the fridge at midnight. Kids say it about themselves as a joke and about others as an insult. The Christian observation: the word touches two things Scripture cares about. The first is gluttony, which the Bible treats as real sin, not a joke: "Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty" (Pro 23:20-21), and Paul warns of those "whose God is their belly" (Php 3:19). Food is a gift to be received with thanks and self-control: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31). The second thing is mockery of others’ bodies, which Scripture forbids: "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth" (Rom 14:3). Calling a heavier classmate "big back" is not a lesson on gluttony; it is contempt. A father can tell a five-year-old: "God gives us yummy food, and we say thank You and eat until we’re full — not too much. And we never make fun of how anyone’s body looks."
webster_summary: TikTok coinage (2023–24) for a heavy eater and "big back behavior" — a joke that touches the real sin of gluttony and slides easily into the sin of mocking another’s body.
webster_full: BIG BACK, n. / a. (TikTok slang, 2023–present; Gen Alpha) A person who eats a lot; describing gluttonous eating. "Ordering two burgers is big back behavior."
Big back behavior — overeating, late-night snacking, excitement over food.
Decode for parents: self-teasing is mostly harmless; aimed at another child, it is body-shaming.
scriptures: Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Rom 14:3
Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.
corruption_summary: Big back makes gluttony a joke and other children’s bodies a target; Scripture treats the first as real sin and the second as forbidden contempt.
corruption_paragraphs: The slang does two opposite things at once. It trivializes a sin — gluttony becomes a funny personality trait — and it weaponizes appearance, so that a heavy child becomes a punchline. Both are formations: one dulls the conscience about appetite, the other trains cruelty about bodies.

Teach the whole truth gently. Food is good, appetite needs ruling, and thanks belong at every meal. Bodies are God’s work and never fair game for mockery. A family table where grace is said, seconds are taken with thought, and no one’s body is ever joked about is the answer to this word.

Whose God is their belly — that’s what gluttony is (Php 3:19).

etymology: A small, flat toy with a ball bearing at its center and two or three weighted lobes that spin between the fingers. Toys of the type existed in the 1990s and 2000s, but the fidget spinner craze of spring 2017 was sudden and total: by May 2017 they filled the best-seller lists, were marketed as aids for focus and anxiety (claims without solid evidence), and were banned by many schools as distractions. The fad faded by the end of the year, leaving the word as shorthand for any sudden toy craze and opening the door for the fidget toys — Pop Its and others — that followed.
biblical_def: A fidget spinner is the little spinning toy every kid had in 2017. It whirred for a few months, filled every classroom, and then vanished into junk drawers. To Gen Alpha it stands for the first great toy craze many of them remember. The Christian observation: the fidget spinner is a perfect small sermon on fads. "The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be... and there is no new thing under the sun" (Ecc 1:9). The thing everyone must have in May is in the drawer by December. And the toy’s whole purpose was restlessness — something for hands that cannot be still. Scripture offers a deeper stillness: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10); "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isa 26:3). A spinning toy is not a sin, and some children truly do focus better with something in their hands. But a heart that is always reaching for the next fidget needs a better rest. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Spinners are fun, and then they get old. God never gets old — He’s always good. When you feel wiggly inside, you can tell Him, and He’ll help your heart be calm."
webster_summary: The bearing-and-lobes spinning toy of the spring 2017 craze — harmless, and a small sermon on fads that pass and on the stillness that knows God.
webster_full: FIDGET SPINNER, n. (toy craze, spring 2017) A small ball-bearing toy with weighted lobes, spun between the fingers. "I have a gold fidget spinner."
Marketed for focus and anxiety; banned in many classrooms as a distraction.
Successors: Pop It, fidget cubes, and other fidget toys.
Decode for parents: harmless; a good occasion to talk about fads.
Webster 1828, the root — SPINNER, n. One that spins; one skilled in spinning.
scriptures: Ecc 1:9
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Php 4:7
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The fidget spinner is a harmless toy; its only lessons are the vanity of the fad and the restlessness it served, which Scripture answers with the peace of a mind stayed on God.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wicked in a spinning toy. The pattern behind it is what deserves notice: a craze that sweeps a school in weeks, a must-have that becomes worthless in months, and a marketing story that sells relief from restlessness. Children who learn early to see that pattern are better guarded against every later fad.

Teach both lessons. Fads pass — there is no new thing under the sun. And the restlessness they promise to soothe has a true remedy: prayer, stillness before God, and "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding" (Php 4:7). A spinner in the hand is fine; a Savior in the heart is better.

Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10).

etymology: A flexible silicone tray of bubbles that can be pushed through and back with a satisfying pop, endlessly. The concept is credited to the Israeli game designers Theo and Ora Coster, who conceived a bubble-popping game decades earlier; a Canadian company released it as a game in 2019, and in 2020–21 TikTok and the pandemic made "Pop Its" the fidget toy of a generation, in every shape and color, traded and collected on playgrounds. "Pop it" also became Gen Alpha shorthand for something satisfying.
biblical_def: A Pop It is the rubbery bubble toy you press to make it pop — then flip and pop again, forever. In 2021 Gen Alpha kids had them in every shape: unicorns, dinosaurs, rainbows. The Christian observation: a Pop It is a toy of small comfort — a little thing for anxious or restless hands — and comfort is something God gives in abundance. David pictured the calm of a child resting: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother" (Psa 131:2). Jesus invites every restless heart: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). And Peter tells us where to put our worries: "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you" (1Pe 5:7). A Pop It is not a sin; it is a toy, and some children with anxious hands are genuinely helped by one. The lesson is to let small comforts point to the great Comforter rather than replace Him. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When you feel worried, you can pop your Pop It — and you can also pop your worries to God, one at a time. He listens to every single one." That is a habit worth starting at five.
webster_summary: The silicone bubble-popping fidget toy (concept credited to Theo and Ora Coster; craze 2020–21) — a small comfort for restless hands, best used to point to the Comforter.
webster_full: POP IT, n. (fidget toy, craze 2020–21) A silicone tray of push-through bubbles. "Can I bring my Pop It to school?"
Variants: shaped Pop Its, keychain Pop Its, Pop It games.
Kid usage: "that’s so pop it" — satisfying.
Decode for parents: harmless; for some anxious children, genuinely calming.
Webster 1828, the root — POP, n. To dart; to start from place to place suddenly.
scriptures: Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: The Pop It is a harmless small comfort; its only snare is the collecting fever of a craze and the habit of reaching for a toy where the soul needs its God.
corruption_paragraphs: Little to correct. Crazes bring collecting envy — the rare color, the giant size — and the fidget-toy industry sells comfort to anxious children as a product. Neither makes the toy wrong, but both are worth naming.

Turn it into prayer practice. A Pop It has many bubbles; a child has many worries. Pop one, name one, give it to God. "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you" (Isa 66:13). The toy can become a little rosary of trust, with no superstition in it — just a child learning to cast her care upon Him.

etymology: A brand of round, marshmallow-soft plush toys launched in 2017 by the toy company Kellytoy (acquired with its brand by Jazwares in 2020), from squish + marshmallow. Each Squishmallow has a name and a little biography on its tag (Wendy the Frog, Cam the Cat), and the line’s hundreds of characters made collecting a craze in 2020–22, with "Squish hunts" through stores, rare editions resold online, and bedrooms walled with plush. Gen Alpha (and many Gen Z teens) call their collections their "squad."
biblical_def: A Squishmallow is the super-soft, round plush animal with a name tag — and a Gen Alpha child often has a whole pile of them. They are for hugging, sleeping with, and collecting. The Christian observation: a soft toy at bedtime is one of the oldest comforts of childhood, and comfort is something God loves to give. He says to His people, "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you" (Isa 66:13), and Paul calls Him "the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" (2Co 1:3). A child hugging a Squishmallow in the dark can be taught to say, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psa 4:8). The caution is the collecting. The brand is designed so there is always another name to find, another rare one to buy, and "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10) — or with plush. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Your Squishmallow is soft and cuddly. But God holds you even better than you hold him — God is the best Comforter." And when the collection grows, he can teach the joy of giving one to a child who has none.
webster_summary: Kellytoy’s named, marshmallow-soft plush (2017; collecting craze 2020–22) — an ancient bedtime comfort that can point to the God of all comfort, and a collecting habit Ecclesiastes warns is never satisfied.
webster_full: SQUISHMALLOW, n. (plush toy brand, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) A round, ultra-soft named plush toy; a collectible. "I have forty Squishmallows."
Vocabulary: squad (one’s collection), Squish hunt (searching stores), rare, squad member.
From squish + marshmallow.
Decode for parents: lovely as comfort; watch the collect-them-all spending.
scriptures: As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort;
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: The Squishmallow is an innocent comfort; its corruption lies only in the collect-them-all design that teaches the heart it is never satisfied.
corruption_paragraphs: Plush toys have comforted children for over a century, and nothing about this line changes that. What is new is the business model: hundreds of named characters, rotating releases, and rarity tiers that turn a cuddly toy into an endless hunt. Children can learn from it that the next one will finally be enough.

Keep the comfort, guard the collecting. Teach contentment with the squad you have, generosity with the extras, and gratitude to the God of all comfort. The best thing a child can learn from a pile of plush is that no pile is the source of peace.

2017: Kellytoy launches the line
2020: Jazwares acquires Kellytoy
2020–22: collecting craze; Squish hunts and resale
Named characters with tag biographies
usage: "This is Cam the Cat. He’s my favorite squad member."
As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you (Isa 66:13).
He that loveth Squishmallows shall not be satisfied with Squishmallows (Ecc 5:10).

etymology: A toothy, rabbit-eared elf creature created by the Hong Kong-born, Belgium-raised artist Kasing Lung for his picture-book series The Monsters (2015), drawing on Nordic folklore. The Chinese toy company Pop Mart began selling Labubu figures in blind boxes in 2019; in 2024 a photo of the K-pop star Lisa with a Labubu bag charm set off a global craze that peaked in 2025, with overnight lines, resale prices in the hundreds of dollars, store fights that led some shops to pause sales, and floods of counterfeits nicknamed "Lafufus." Online rumors calling Labubu a demon idol spread at the same time; the creator describes it as a mischievous forest elf.
biblical_def: A Labubu is the little furry monster with a big toothy grin that Gen Alpha (and their older sisters) clip to their backpacks. In 2025 everyone wanted one, people waited in long lines, and some paid huge prices. The Christian observation: a Christian family should be careful to aim its concern at the right thing. Many viral posts said Labubus were demons or idols. Scripture tells us not to be ruled by that fear: "we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one" (1Co 8:4). A toy elf has no power. But Scripture does name an idolatry that the Labubu craze shows in full: "covetousness, which is idolatry" (Col 3:5). The lines, the fights, the resale prices, the fake ones, the fear of missing out — that is the real idol, and it lives in the heart, not in the plastic. Jesus said, "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15), and the Preacher said the lover of abundance is never satisfied with increase (Ecc 5:10). A father can tell a five-year-old: "A Labubu is just a toy — it can’t hurt you. But wanting stuff so much that we’re grumpy without it can hurt our hearts. Jesus is better than any toy."
webster_summary: Kasing Lung’s toothy elf (2015), sold by Pop Mart in blind boxes (2019-) and a global craze in 2024–25 — not a demon, as rumor said, but a showcase of the covetousness Scripture calls idolatry.
webster_full: LABUBU, proper n. (collectible character, 2015; Pop Mart craze 2024–25) The rabbit-eared, sharp-toothed elf figure and plush, sold in blind boxes and as bag charms. "I got a Labubu in the new series!"
Vocabulary: Lafufu (counterfeit), secret or chase (the rare figure in a series), bag charm.
From Kasing Lung’s The Monsters picture books (2015).
Decode for parents: not a demon; the real danger is the buying frenzy and the blind-box gamble.
scriptures: As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: The Labubu panic aimed at the wrong idol: the toy is nothing, but the craze around it — lines, fights, resale, counterfeits — is covetousness, which is idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: Christians online spent much of 2025 debating whether Labubu was a demon. That debate missed the point Scripture makes plainly: idols are nothing, and the true danger is the heart’s worship. The craze’s real fruit was envy, debt, scarcity panic, and children taught that a status object is worth a fight in a store.

Answer the right question. Do not teach your child to fear a toy; teach her to rule her wants. Make a rule of waiting before buying, of giving before getting, of contentment spoken aloud. If she owns one, let it be a toy and nothing more. The heart that can hold a Labubu loosely has learned Colossians 3:5.
roots_summary: Kasing Lung’s The Monsters (2015) → Pop Mart blind boxes (2019) → Lisa photo (2024) → global craze and "Lafufu" counterfeits (2025).

An idol is nothing in the world — but covetousness is idolatry (1Co 8:4; Col 3:5).
A man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of Labubus (Luk 12:15).

etymology: A sealed package containing one figure from a series, without showing which; the buyer learns what he got only after opening it, and one "secret" or "chase" figure is far rarer than the rest. The format descends from Japanese capsule-toy vending (gachapon, from the 1960s) and was made a global business by the Chinese company Pop Mart (blind boxes from the mid-2010s) and by children’s brands such as L.O.L. Surprise! (2016). Video-game "loot boxes," which work the same way, have been ruled a form of gambling in some countries; Gen Alpha meets the mechanism first in a toy aisle.
biblical_def: A blind box is a mystery package: you pay, you open, and only then do you find out which toy you got — and there’s always a super-rare one you probably didn’t get. Gen Alpha children love the surprise and beg for "just one more." The Christian observation: the blind box is a gentle form of the same machine as a slot machine. The thrill is not the toy; it is the chance. Scripture does not treat chance as a god to be courted. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33): God rules what we call luck. And Scripture warns about money spent chasing a lucky outcome: "Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase" (Pro 13:11), and "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare" (1Ti 6:9). The blind box also trains the heart that is never satisfied: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Mystery boxes are fun surprises, but they’re made so we always want one more. Let’s pick a toy we can see and be happy with it — and remember God gives us good gifts on purpose, not by luck."
webster_summary: Mystery-package collectible (gachapon 1960s; Pop Mart and L.O.L. Surprise! 2010s) with a rare "secret" figure — a child’s first gambling mechanism, in a world where the lot’s whole disposing is of the LORD.
webster_full: BLIND BOX, n. (collectible packaging, 2010s–present; Gen Alpha usage) A sealed package holding an unknown figure from a series. "I opened three blind boxes and got the same one twice."
Vocabulary: secret / chase (the rare figure), series, unboxing, duplicate.
Relatives: gachapon (Japanese capsule toys), loot box (video games).
Decode for parents: the draw is the gamble, not the toy; set limits before the aisle.
Webster 1828, the root — BLIND, a. Destitute of the sense of seeing, either by natural defect, or by deprivation; not having sight.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: The blind box sells the thrill of chance to children and trains the never-satisfied heart; Scripture places every lot in God’s hand and warns against wealth chased by vanity.
corruption_paragraphs: The blind-box design is not accidental. Uncertainty releases more excitement than certainty, and a rare chase figure keeps a buyer opening box after box. Regulators in some countries treat the same mechanism in video games as gambling. In the toy aisle it shapes children who have not yet learned what is happening to them.

Teach your child to see the machine. Count together how many boxes it would take to get the secret one; compare the cost to buying the toy outright. Then teach the theology: God rules the lot, and good gifts come from Him on purpose. A child who learns to enjoy a known gift is free of the casino’s first lesson.
roots_summary: Japanese gachapon capsule toys (1960s-) → Pop Mart blind boxes (2010s) and L.O.L. Surprise! (2016) → Gen Alpha collectible format; cousin of the loot box.

etymology: Not the hockey trophy (1892) but the Stanley Quencher, a 40-ounce insulated tumbler with a handle and straw made by the Stanley company (founded 1913). Revived in 2019–20 through a partnership with women-run shopping bloggers, it became in 2023–24 the status object of tween and teen girls: in November 2023 a viral video showed a Quencher with ice still inside after a car fire (the company replaced the owner’s car), and in January 2024 limited-edition releases brought overnight lines and scuffles at Target. Girls collected them in many colors, decorated them, and called them "Stanleys" or "Stanley cups."
biblical_def: To Gen Alpha girls, a Stanley cup is not a hockey trophy — it’s the giant water tumbler with a handle that everybody had to have, in every color, in 2023 and 2024. The Christian observation: a cup is one of Scripture’s richest images, and the Stanley craze shows the oldest problem with cups — caring about the outside. Jesus told the Pharisees, "ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess" (Mat 23:25), and "cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also" (Mat 23:26). The Stanley trend made the cup’s outside — the brand, the color, the stickers — the whole point. But Jesus also made a cup of water one of the holiest things in the world: "whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward" (Mat 10:42). And He offered a drink no tumbler can hold: "whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst" (Joh 4:14). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Water cups are good — God made water! The best thing to do with a cup is share a drink with someone who’s thirsty. Jesus says that’s a big deal to Him."
webster_summary: The Stanley Quencher tumbler, tween status object of 2023–24 (car-fire video, Target lines) — the outside of the cup made the whole point, against Christ’s cup of cold water and the living water.
webster_full: STANLEY CUP, n. (Gen Alpha / Gen-Z usage, 2023–present) The Stanley Quencher, a 40-oz insulated tumbler; a status accessory. "I want the pink Stanley for my birthday."
Also Stanley, Stanley tumbler. Accessories: straw toppers, name stickers, "boots" for the base.
Not to be confused with the National Hockey League trophy (1892).
Decode for parents: a water bottle is good; a water bottle as a ranking of girls is the problem.
Webster 1828, the root — CUP, n. A small vessel of capacity, used commonly to drink out of.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.
And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
corruption_summary: The Stanley craze made a water tumbler’s outside — brand, color, scarcity — the measure of a girl’s belonging; Christ cleanses the inside of the cup and sanctifies the cup of cold water given away.
corruption_paragraphs: Status objects for children are not new, but the Stanley craze showed how fast one can form: a few viral videos, a scarcity release, and suddenly a ten-year-old with the wrong tumbler feels left out. Girls collected multiples, and the cup became a badge of being in. That is respect of persons by accessory, and envy by color.

Turn the cup inside out. Teach your daughter that what fills her is what matters, that her worth is not in what she carries, and that the most Christlike thing she can do with any cup is offer a drink to someone thirsty. Then tell her about the living water. A girl who knows that well will not need a forty-ounce badge.

etymology: A 2023–24 label, from the cosmetics chain Sephora, for tweens — roughly eight to twelve — who flood beauty stores for luxury skincare and makeup, often products made for adult or aging skin (retinol serums, acid peels) and brands made famous on TikTok. Viral videos from store employees and shoppers described crowds of children testing products and filming "get ready with me" routines, and dermatologists warned about irritated young skin. "Sephora kid" became shorthand for a child in a hurry to look older.
biblical_def: A Sephora kid is a girl, often eight to twelve, who wants expensive grown-up skincare and makeup — the brands she sees in TikTok videos — and spends her birthday money at the beauty store. The Christian observation: most of what is happening here is a child in a hurry to be older, and Scripture says there is a time for everything: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecc 3:1). Childhood is a season God gave, not a waiting room. Paul says, "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child" (1Co 13:11) — and that was right for that time. The skincare itself is not sin; cleanliness and care are good. But the anti-aging serum on a nine-year-old face says something false: that her face is already a problem to fix. Scripture says otherwise: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14), and the adornment God prizes is "the hidden man of the heart... the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Your face is perfect for being five! God made you just right. You don’t need grown-up stuff — you need to be a happy kid who loves Jesus." He can tell the ten-year-old the same thing, with a trip for ice cream instead of serum.
webster_summary: 2023–24 label for tweens buying adult and anti-aging skincare at beauty stores — a child rushed out of her season and taught her face is a problem, against "fearfully and wonderfully made."
webster_full: SEPHORA KID, n. (Gen Alpha / Gen-Z usage, 2023–present) A tween who shops for luxury and adult skincare and makeup, often inspired by social media. "The store was full of Sephora kids."
Related: GRWM (get ready with me), skincare routine, glass skin, preppy.
Decode for parents: the products can irritate young skin; the bigger issue is the message that she must look older.
scriptures: Ecc 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: The Sephora-kid trend hurries little girls out of childhood and into the anxieties of aging skin; Scripture gives every season its time and prizes the hidden ornament of the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The phenomenon is a commercial and cultural pull on young girls: influencers sell routines, brands design packaging that appeals to children, and social feeds make an expensive serum a badge of belonging. The message beneath it is that a child’s face needs fixing and that being older is better. Both are lies that grow with the girl.

Protect the season. Let your daughter be a child; teach simple care (wash, sunscreen, rest); and speak often about her worth before God. Praise her kindness more than her looks. A girl who is secure in being "fearfully and wonderfully made" at nine is less likely to be at war with the mirror at nineteen.
roots_summary: Sephora (French cosmetics chain, 1969) + kid → TikTok-era tween beauty trend (2023–24).

Dermatologists warn about adult actives on young skin
usage: "Can I get the retinol serum?" "You’re nine. Your face is perfect for nine."
To every thing there is a season — and childhood is one (Ecc 3:1).
The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is of great price (1Pe 3:4).

etymology: A translation of the Korean beauty term yuri pibu ("glass skin"), naming a face so clear, smooth, and dewy that it seems to reflect light like glass. The phrase went viral through Korean-beauty ("K-beauty") influencers around 2017–18, attached to multi-step skincare routines and later to photo filters that create the look artificially. For Gen Alpha girls, glass skin is the goal of the skincare routine and the look of the filtered face.
biblical_def: Glass skin means skin so smooth and shiny it looks like glass — the look girls see in videos and filters and try to copy with lots of skincare steps. The Christian observation: glass is a beautiful word in Scripture, and it is never about our faces. The heavenly city’s street "was pure gold, as it were transparent glass" (Rev 21:21) — the glory belongs to God’s dwelling. And the Bible’s best use of glass is as a mirror: "we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory" (2Co 3:18). The face God is making glorious is the one turned toward Him. James warns about looking in a mirror and forgetting: a man "beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was" (Jas 1:24). The filtered face is a glass that lies. Real faces have pores, freckles, and lines — and every one of them is God’s handiwork. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Your skin is beautiful just the way God made it — freckles and all! The Bible says when we look at Jesus, He makes us shine on the inside." That is the only glass skin that lasts.
webster_summary: Korean beauty ideal yuri pibu (viral c. 2017–18) of dewy, poreless skin, now a filter look — while Scripture keeps glass for God’s city and for the mirror in which we behold His glory and are changed.
webster_full: GLASS SKIN, n. (K-beauty term, c. 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) Extremely clear, smooth, luminous skin, as if made of glass; the goal of many skincare routines. "Her skin is literally glass skin."
From Korean yuri pibu, glass skin.
Related: dewy, skincare routine, Sephora kid, beauty filters.
Decode for parents: much of what children see is filtered; real skin is not glass.
Webster 1828, the root — GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies.
Webster 1828, the root — SKIN, n. The natural covering of animal bodies, consisting of the cuticle or scarf-skin, the rete mucosum, and the cutis or hide.
scriptures: And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
Jas 1:23
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
Jas 1:24
For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.
corruption_summary: Glass skin sets a filtered, poreless ideal before girls whose real faces cannot meet it; Scripture keeps glass for God’s glory and the mirror that changes us into Christ’s image.
corruption_paragraphs: The ideal is not wicked in itself — clear skin is pleasant, and care is good. The trouble is that the standard is partly unreal, built from filters and editing, and children cannot tell the difference. Girls are taught to see normal skin as a flaw and to spend time, money, and worry chasing a surface that does not exist.

Tell your daughter the truth about filters, and tell her a better truth about glass. The glory Scripture promises is not on the skin but in the soul, as we behold the Lord and are changed. Pray with her in front of a mirror sometimes, thanking God for the face He made.
